lesson.title: Dividing the Land: The Dawes Act and the Assault on Tribal Sovereignty
lesson.summary: In 1887, Congress replaced communal tribal landholding with individual, privately owned plots in a supposedly reformist law that stripped Native nations of roughly two thirds of their remaining land within a generation.
lesson.body:
By the mid 1880s, with most Plains nations confined to reservations and armed resistance largely broken, described in the earlier chapters on the Native American Wars and the Battle of Little Bighorn, federal policy shifted from open warfare to a different strategy aimed at breaking up Native nations from within. The new target was the very foundation of the societies described in the chapter on Indigenous North American Cultures: communal landholding, extended kinship networks, and tribal systems of governance that had sustained Native communities for generations.

The Dawes Severalty Act, also called the General Allotment Act, passed in 1887 and sponsored by Senator Henry Dawes of Massachusetts, authorized the president to divide reservation land, previously held collectively by each tribe, into individual family allotments, typically up to 160 acres for the head of a household and smaller parcels for others. Some reformers who supported the law sincerely believed they were helping Native people by pushing them toward individual land ownership and settled farming, on the assumption that this would speed assimilation into white American economic and social norms. Allottees were granted U.S. citizenship, and their land was held in a federal trust for twenty five years, nominally to prevent immediate sale.

The result was catastrophic for Native landholding. Once individual family allotments were carved out of a reservation, the government declared the remaining acreage "surplus," land that had belonged to the tribe as a whole, and opened it to purchase by white settlers, railroads, and speculators. Because most reservations held far less land than would have been needed to allot every family a full 160 acres, and because the trust protections were frequently circumvented or later lifted outright, enormous amounts of land left Native hands in a very short time. Tribal landholdings nationwide fell from roughly 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million acres by 1934, when the policy was finally abandoned under the Indian Reorganization Act, a loss of roughly two thirds of all remaining Native land in under fifty years.

Allotment worked alongside other assimilation policies of the same period, most notoriously government and church run boarding schools far from reservations, such as the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, founded in 1879, which forcibly separated Native children from their families and punished them for speaking their own languages or practicing their own customs. The school's founder, Richard Henry Pratt, summarized the underlying philosophy bluntly as an effort to "kill the Indian" culturally in order to "save the man." Together, allotment and forced assimilation created the atmosphere of loss and desperation out of which the religious movement covered in the next chapter emerged.
